claims.text: Applying a thin, conformal ZrC coating to boride-based components will improve their resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion.
The ZrC coating will act as a chemically inert, high-temperature barrier between molten aluminum and the boride substrate.
HfB2 and similar borides are high-melting-point materials.
Typical microstructural features in boride-based components can permit localized diffusion and reaction with molten aluminum.
CVD deposition of ZrC can produce a dense, adherent surface layer on the boride substrate.
The ZrC coating should remain protective at approximately 660°C during prolonged molten-aluminum exposure if it retains adhesion and integrity.
The ZrC layer will form a uniform, defect-reduced barrier.
The ZrC barrier will limit aluminum diffusion into the boride substrate.
The ZrC barrier will suppress the formation of deleterious aluminum-boride interfacial phases.
ZrC has high chemical stability at elevated temperatures.
Adding ZrC to a chemically deposited Ni-P nanocomposite coating on N80 steel reduced coating defects and improved corrosion and wear resistance.
A continuous ZrC coating will prevent reactive molten aluminum from interacting with the underlying boride phase.
ZrC-coated boride samples will have a significantly lower molten-aluminum corrosion rate than uncoated boride samples.
ZrC-coated samples will exhibit reduced weight loss and lower corrosion current densities after molten-aluminum exposure.
ZrC-coated samples will retain a more intact surface microstructure after molten-aluminum exposure than uncoated samples.
Poor coating adhesion, excessive thermal cycling, or sufficiently long exposure can degrade the coating and reduce its protective effectiveness.
Analogous evidence suggests a potential 30–50% reduction in corrosion metrics.
The magnitude of improvement for boride components in molten aluminum remains uncertain pending direct testing.
